choices: Sign your name at the bottom of the form.
Your signature at the bottom of the form.
If you sign at the bottom of the form.
Signing your name at the bottom of the form.
answer: Sign your name at the bottom of the form.
hints: One choice looks like it has no subject, but it is a command. In a command, the subject "you" is understood.
Check each choice for a real verb. Then check whether it starts with a word like "if" that leaves the thought unfinished.

A command such as "Close the door." is complete because its subject is understood to be "you". A noun with no verb, an "if" part with no main idea, and an -ing phrase alone are all fragments. Test each choice.

solution.methodName: Check for subject, verb and complete thought

steps.action: "Sign your name at the bottom of the form." is a command. Its subject, "you", is understood: "(You) sign your name …".
steps.why: A command gives an order or an instruction. English leaves out the "you", but the sentence is still complete.

steps.action: It has a verb (sign) and a complete thought, so it is a complete sentence.
"Your signature at the bottom of the form." has no verb. It is a fragment.
"If you sign at the bottom of the form." starts with "if", so it waits for a result that never comes. It is a fragment.
"Signing your name at the bottom of the form." has no subject and only an -ing word. It is a fragment.
The complete sentence is "Sign your name at the bottom of the form."

trapNotes.Your signature at the bottom of the form: It reads like an instruction printed on a form, but it has no verb. It is only a noun with a phrase after it.
It has a subject and a verb ("you sign"), but "If" means a result must follow. If you sign, then what?
trapNotes.Signing your name at the bottom of the f: This looks like the command with a few changes. But an -ing word alone is not a full verb, and there is no subject.
